reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey is the only source here with a measured adoption figure for the sector. It puts AI use in Educational services (NAICS 61) at 30.0% of firms, down from 35.5% in the prior period, based on firms answering yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks. The survey first asked the question in September 2023. That is the whole of the measured picture in this material, and it describes firms in the education sector generally rather than schools or universities specifically.

The Department of Education issued the federal guidance, and its page is the most concrete account of what AI is actually used for. It publishes an inventory of the Department's own AI use-cases, including CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics and intelligent automation, Grammarly for written communication, Otter.AI for real-time transcription and meeting collaboration, and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. The listed tasks are largely administrative and instructional support: generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in several programming languages, extracting key points and action items from public documents, generating mock data sets for testing, training employees on prompt engineering, converting data types such as a county name into its FIPS code, drafting job descriptions and qualifications, and composing outreach messages. This site's own coverage of the sector describes tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy from K-12 through university.

On regulation, the Department of Education frames its guidance around permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education, and its OCIO supports adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement and responsible and secure usage, in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The page also notes testing of filters and data loss prevention against fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information, which is the only risk-control practice described in the material.

Courses and certifications are catalogued here, and that catalog is the clearest evidence of where the learning market sits. It lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each and re-verified daily. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The catalog distinguishes university courses as generally structured around exam-driven theory and the industry courses as code-first or hands-on, and it states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy as a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning. Its page describes sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand and forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, quantifying impact with rubrics, ratings and scoring, and powering policy, procurement and investment decisions, along with mapping competitive and partnership landscapes. It does not publish specific adoption or spending figures for education AI in the excerpt available here.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow set of conclusions. The Census Bureau figure gives a sector-level adoption rate and shows it moving down between periods, not up. The Department of Education inventory shows that the documented uses are mostly drafting, summarizing, transcribing, coding assistance, and internal analysis rather than student-facing instruction. None of these sources report ROI evidence, cost savings, or outcome improvements from education AI, so there is nothing here to cite on that front. The regulatory posture is guidance and adherence to federal rules rather than a settled compliance regime, and the course catalog shows a training market split between free industry material and university graduate courses, with no completion or enrollment data to judge which path people actually finish.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
